results.title: Development of Translational Pharmacokinetic–Pharmacodynamic Models - PMC
results.content: Mechanism-based PD models, therefore, frequently reflect an integration of the basic components to describe and understand the complex interplay between the pharmacology of drug action and the (patho-)physiological control systems.7,8 One example is the target-mediated PK–PD model developed for interferon-β1a in monkeys.9 This model includes receptor binding as a key factor in both PK and PD processes and utilizes a precursor-dependent indirect response model to capture the induction of neopterin (a classic biomarker of interferon-β receptor agonism) in concordance with known mechanisms. For example, the model developed for interferon-β1a in monkeys was shown to characterize its PK–PD properties well in human male volunteers.9,17 This was not unexpected, given that most of the mechanisms and processes emulated by the model appear to be largely conserved across species, a feature often shared for many macromolecules.15 Although the structural nature of PBPK models makes them uniquely suited for scaling and predicting human drug exposures, the extrapolation of PK–PD models from animals to humans is primarily based on classical allometric relationships. Brodie and colleagues were the first to examine some PK–PD properties across species, demonstrating interspecies differences in global terms such as duration of action and half-life, but similarities in plasma concentration on awakening following hexobarbital administration.26 There has long been a case made for the usefulness of studying drug effects in preclinical models, and a general belief that the plasma drug concentration required for eliciting a certain (intensity of) action (e.g., EC50) is often similar in experimental animals and humans.27 While interspecies differences in relative receptor affinity and plasma protein binding often exist,28 several examples show reasonable concordance of such properties between rats and humans for congeneric series of drugs. Interspecies scaling has been applied to complex PK–PD models, including the hypothermic and cortisol responses to buspirone and flesinoxan (two 5-HT1A receptor agonists)32 and the effects of erythropoietin on reticulocytes, red blood cells, and hemoglobin levels in humans.33 Despite the relative complexity of the models, their diverse structural components, and the differences in the molecular sizes of the drugs, the prevailing observations were that: (i) PK and physiological turnover parameters obeyed allometric principles, and (ii) pharmacological capacity and sensitivity parameters were essentially species-independent.

Nonclinical Research Central Laboratory Services Real World Data Order a Kit Contact Us. ## Managing Your Health. ## Diseases & Therapeutic Areas. ## Treatment Modalities & Methods. ## Scientific Lab Disciplines. ## Labs. ## Industries. # PK / PD modeling. PK/PD modeling is the integration of pharmacokinetics with a response. The response may be positive (such as a biomarker being targeted or desired efficacy); or the response may be negative (such as a toxicological endpoint). PK/PD modeling allows for prediction of the desired or undesired response, based on a particular administered dose or measure of exposure. ## PK / PD Modeling Overview. * Conducted using either a compartmental PK model or a PBPK model. * Applies to both small and large molecules. * Often combined with scaling to develop a predictive PK/PD human model. ## Common Uses. * Interspecies scaling / Phase I exposure predictions. * Assessment of potential impacts on efficacy from PK changes (due to material lot changes). * Preclinical & clinical optimization study design. ## Regulatory Guidance & Timing. PK/PD modeling is not specifically required in regulatory guidance, but the FDA has strongly suggested including modeling in the data package. In addition, the 2017 EMA guideline for first-in-human (FIH) dosing recommends that estimation of FIH should be based on state-of-the-art modeling (e.g. PK/PD and PBPK) and or using allometric factors. A PK/PD model can be critical for predicting FIH doses of large molecules with approaches using a minimally anticipated biological effect level (MABEL) or a pharmacologically active dose (PAD). PK / PD modeling studies typically occur during late discovery through clinical. ### Related Content. * *In vivo* PK & pharmacology studies. * *In vitro* cell assays, specifically investigating pharmacology.

Sygnature Discovery’s DMPK modelling and simulation services support confident, data-driven decision-making from early discovery through translational development. By combining *in vitro* data, *in vivo* insights and advanced computational tools- including physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling – we help researchers optimize dose selection, study design and progression strategies with greater precision and confidence. In early drug discovery, screening cascades involve evaluating compounds across a structured panel of *in vitro* assays to assess potency, selectivity and potential safety risks. At Sygnature Discovery, we apply mechanistic modelling techniques to translate *in vitro* results into actionable dosing recommendations for pharmacodynamic (PD) studies. PBPK modelling plays a pivotal role in predicting human pharmacokinetics based on preclinical data. By integrating physiological parameters, drug-specific properties and mechanistic ADME insights, PBPK models simulate how a drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted in the human body. In addition to guiding internal drug discovery programs, our modelling and simulation services support strategic decision during in-licensing or out-licensing activities. Through mechanistic analysis, PBPK modelling and PK/PD simulations, we help assess a compound’s viability in the drug discovery process. results.title: Translational PBPK/PD modeling in drug discovery: A CRO ...
results.content: The use of translational physiologically based pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic (PBPK/PD) modeling has become a standard practice in drug discovery, providing advanced data integration accounting for species-specific physiology and target pharmacology. This paper provides a preclinical contract research organization (CRO) perspective on the applications, benefits, and challenges of translational PBPK/PD modeling approaches in integrated drug discovery (IDD) collaborations. Although sponsors retain intellectual property rights and maintain final authority over key decisions, CRO experts serve as discipline leaders, driving the science and managing logistics with full access and contribution to the project strategy.9 The discipline of drug metabolism and pharmacokinetics (DMPK) plays a key role within IDD projects by integrating data from multiple sources (i.e. _in silico_, _in vitro_, and _in vivo_), and often from multiple sites, to predict human pharmacokinetics (PK).10 Moreover, PK data must be integrated with pharmacodynamics (PD) and Tox data for efficacy predictions and safety risk assessments. Over the past decade, translational physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) and pharmacodynamic (PBPK/PD) modeling and simulation have emerged as valuable tools for these tasks.[11], [12], [13], [14] In this perspective article we describe the use of these tools in drug discovery from a CRO viewpoint, highlighting how such approaches can enhance project success rates and add significant value to the sponsor–CRO collaboration. Today, DPRs are an integral part of drug discovery teams and the main personnel responsible for designing the DMPK _in vitro/in vivo_ screening cascade, overseeing the PK/PD strategy, evaluating PK requirements, and integrating PK/PD data.[10], [43] Predictably, the figure of the DPR first appeared in large pharmaceutical companies because of the growing In large pharmaceutical companies, the role of DPR is often well defined and well represented, with specialized PBPK/PD modeling and simulation experts available internally. * E.P.
